column4: At death, angels strike the disbelievers’ faces and backs and tell them to taste the punishment of the Burning Fire; this joins the section’s dictionary account of ع ذ ب as striking to an explicit punishment scene.
This repeats the angels’ striking of faces and backs when taking souls; it is a parallel bodily blow to the strike behind the section’s whip image, though this verse does not name torment.
This is the left-handed record that identifies the person taken and shackled in 69:30; the row’s own detail is the judgment scene that begins that restraint sequence.

The condemned says his wealth did not avail him; this adds the failure of wealth immediately before the authority-loss and shackling in 69:29–30, against the section’s mention of hoarded wealth and neglect of the poor.
The condemned says his authority has departed; that makes the fall from worldly power explicit before the restraint order in 69:30, a sharp reversal of Pharaoh’s coercive authority.

Dhul-Qarnayn sets iron pieces in a gap and pours molten metal over them to seal a barrier; this is a specific worldly act of fastening and containment, used to protect rather than punish, beside the section’s peg and binding images.
After the shackles and fire in 73:12, this adds choking food and painful torment; it supplies another bodily form in the passage’s combination of punishments.
After the criminals bound in chains in 14:49, their clothing is pitch and fire covers their faces; this adds a material bodily torment to that restraint scene.
After the boiling-water pour and iron maces in 22:19–21, those who try to leave the Fire are returned to it; the verse adds that their punishment allows no escape.
Criminals are recognized and seized by their forelocks and feet; this is a specific forced bodily restraint parallel to the section’s feet-in-fetters dictionary sense and its unmatchable binding.
Following the punishment and the failure to feed the poor in 69:34, the condemned receives only foul food; that reverses his withholding of food into his own deprivation.
This specifies that only sinners eat the foul food of 69:36, completing the passage’s link between wrongdoing, neglected feeding, and punishment.
The closing rebuke says they withhold even small acts of aid; it sharpens the same withholding of care that the section links from 69:34 to 89:18.
After the feeding and fear in 76:8–10, God protects the righteous from that day’s evil; this contrasts the chained punishment cited from 76:4 with safety on the same day.
The next ayah rewards their patience with a garden and silk clothing, a concrete release from the chains and fire named earlier in the same surah.

The steep path includes caring for an orphan of close relation; this complements 90:14’s feeding and reverses the failure to honor the orphan in 89:17, the surrounding context of the section’s poor-feeding link.
The next recipient is a person in misery and need; this specifies whom the feeding path serves, against the neglect condemned around 89:18.

After poured water, earth-splitting, and grain in 80:25–27, the passage names grapes and fodder; it continues the beneficial harvest produced by the same root ص ب ب that the section uses for punishment.
The watered growth continues with olives and date palms; this is another concrete provision from the section’s root ص ب ب in its contrasting, life-giving use.
The passage next names dense gardens, continuing the crop scene after the abundant water of 80:25 and contrasting it with a punitive pour.
Fruit and pasture complete the produce list begun after the poured water; the verse continues the same root’s beneficial result.
The passage concludes that the crops are provision for people and livestock; this completes the positive purpose of the pour whose punitive counterpart the section develops.
The people of the left are in scorching wind and boiling water; this is a specific pairing of torments that illuminates the section’s dictionary gloss of mixed kinds of punishment.
The next ayah adds a shade of black smoke to the scorching wind and boiling water in 56:42, extending that mixture of torments.
The smoke’s shade is neither cool nor beneficial; this completes the sequence’s varied but unrelieving punishment.
This punishment is boiling water and foul discharge; it gives a specific pairing to the section’s source gloss that the whip points to mixed kinds of torment.
The following ayah adds other punishments of the same kind; it explicitly continues the variety described in 38:57.
The passage identifies the punishment as a blazing fire; the next verse specifies its bodily effect, making it relevant to the section’s physical image of torment.
The flame strips the skin from the head; this is a direct bodily counterpart to the section’s dictionary description of braided leather entering the skin and to its account of severe pain.
The Fire calls those who turned away; this gives the punishment in 70:15–16 an active, pursuing force rather than a passive location.

The same description identifies those who amassed and hoarded wealth; this brings hoarding into the account of the people pursued by punishment, as in the section’s surrounding verses on wealth and feeding the poor.
The righteous keep a known share of their wealth for those who ask and those deprived; this directly reverses the section’s rebuke for failing to urge food for the poor.
This specifies the recipients of that share as the asker and deprived person; it completes the charitable contrast to the poor-feeding failure linked by the section.

Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, then ordered into the severest punishment at the Hour; this directly answers Pharaoh’s claim to lasting torment with his own people’s continuing judgment.
